data.title: A new cell signal required for patterning and morphogenesis downstream of EGFR-Ras.
data.description: Our previous work has shown that Proximal-Distal (PD) leg development in Drosophila melanogaster proceeds stepwise from small presumptive regions to the definition of the final PD leg pattern, and has suggested that a new developmental cascade involving several classes of PD genes is driving at least three different aspects of PD patterning and growth. Having elucidated the later-acting of these processes, namely leg segmentation, we plan in this proposal to unravel two earlier-acting PD processes, which are 1) Tarsal growth and patterning, and 2) early PD patterning. 1. To understand tarsal growth and patterning, we plan to ascertain the role of EGFR-Ras signalling in PD leg development by analysing: 1.1) the co-ordination of leg patterning and growth by EFGR ligands; 1.2) the identity and molecular mechanisms of the effectors which mediate EGFR-Ras signalling in legs, and 1.3) the interaction of Notch and EGFR-Ras signalling to form leg joints. 2. To understand early PD patterning we plan to analyse: 2.1) the role of cell communication in early PD patterning; 2.2) the PD cell signalling processes mediated by known signalling proteins, and 2.3) the identity and molecular nature of other gene products involved in early PD patterning. Our objective is to obtain a complete picture of PD leg development and of its links with other limb developmental processes. We expect the results of this project to have a wide relevance since several aspects of Drosophila limb patterning are conserved in vertebrate limb development. Even if some of our expectations are not fulfilled, the new genes, regulatory effects and signalling mechanisms characterised by us will have a direct bearing on other areas of Drosophila and vertebrate biology.

data.title: Functional genomics of type 2 diabetes quantitative trait loci in rat models.
data.Sponsor(s): Prof Peter Donnelly, Prof Anthony Monaco
data.description: The focus of my research is to identify genes leading to diabetes and atherosclerosis in the spontaneously diabetic Goto-Kakisaki (GK) rat strain, a model for human non insulin dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM). In a recent genetic study performed in a GKxBN intercross we mapped in 7 large chromosomal regions susceptibility loci that are independently responsible for the control of physiological parameters relevant to NIDDM. The aim of the proposed research is to identify genes at these loci using both genetic and molecular biology approaches. Genetic markers will be used for fine characterisation of a series of congenic strains for each locus linked to a diabetic phenotype in order to define the smallest segment likely to contain the train-causing allele. Congenic lines derived from the GK rat and from the Spontaneously Hypertensive (SHR) rats for similar chromosomal segments will be investigated for a wide range of phenotypes relevant to diabetes and atherosclerosis in order to test a possible pleiotropic effect of these genes. Subsequent positional cloning methodologies will be applied to isolate genes in well defined chromosomal regions and to identify regions of homology in the human genome. Results from genetic investigations performed in the GK and SHR rats should allow us to isolate specific susceptibility genes which can be tested as candidates for NIDDM and hypertension in human.

data.title: Mechanisms that maintain neural progenitors and control neurogenesis in Xenopus embryos.
data.description: The first step in vertebrate neural development is the induction of neuroepithelium from ectoderm which would have otherwise formed epidermis. Within this neuroepithelium, neurons differentiate in defined positions. Although controlling where neuronal differentiation takes place is crucial for generating a functional nervous system, little is known about how this spatial control is achieved. Previously, I have shown that XBF-1, an anterior neural plate specific transcription factor, is likely to play a role in the spatial control of neurogenesis. I have shown that in normal development neurogenesis is positioned around the anterior boundary of the expression domain of XBF-1. Furthermore, I have shown that XBF-1 represses or promotes neuronal differentiation at high or low concentrations respectively and that when it is misexpressed in the posterior neural plate, endogenous neuronal differentiation is re-positioned at the boundary of high- XBF-1 expressing ectoderm. In this proposal I intend to exploit this observation in order to understand how neurogenesis is spatially controlled. First, I will investigate whether neurogenesis takes place at the boundary of XBF-1 expressing ectoderm by a mechanism that is i) dose dependent and cell autonomous or (ii) cell non- autonomous and if so, what is the inducing signal. Second, I will characterise direct targets of XBF-1 in the anterior neural plate in order to understand i) how XBF-1 affects neural development at the molecular level and ii) how cells respond to different concentrations of XBF-1. Third, since expression of XBF-1 is restricted to the anterior neural plate, I will undertake a functional screen to identify genes that define the sites of neurogenesis in the posterior neural plate.

data.title: Functional modelling of defective WASp activity.
data.description: · Woskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is a severe X-linked recessive disease characterised by microthrombocytopenia, eczema and immune deficiency. Biochemical data from several laboratories, including our own, suggest that the protein product of the gene mutated in WAS (WASP) plays a role in regulating changes in the architecture of the actin cytoskeleton in response to external stimuli. However, for some primary immunodeficiencies (PIDs) such as the Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS), our understanding of basic gene function and pathophysiological consequences of mutation remains limited, and the application of novel molecular therapies is not yet possible. Although curable by stem cell transplantation, the complications associated with this procedure for WAS are greater than those encountered with other PIDs, and the development of alternative therapeutic strategies based on somatic gene transfer may therefore be particularly important. The objectives of this application are to investigate the cellular biology of WAS, particularly in terms of immune and stem cell trafficking, and to translate this into the development of successful molecular therapies based on somatic gene transfer. This proposal will investigate the following areas: The contribution of dendritic cell and stem cell trafficking defects to the WAS phenotype in models developed by gene targeting. The feasibility of retroviral and lentiviral vector gene transfer to stem cells and to mature cell populations for therapy of WAS in vivo.

data.title: Facility for the Evaluation of Infectious Particles.
data.description: The proposal is to build and equip a unique facility for the biophysical analysis of pathogens by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and mass spectrometry within ACDP Class 3 containment. This facility will: facilitate an interdisciplinary environment in which structural, immunological and viral approaches fuse. complement and support X-ray crystallographic analyses at contained synchrotron beamlines. have the facilities and infrastructure to provide a national and international centre for the evaluation of infectious particles. The facility will provide a unique opportunity to exploit cutting- edge research interests in the structural analysis of pathogens and viral receptors already firmly established in the Oxford Centre for Molecular Science (OCMS) affiliated laboratories of Professors D. Stuart, Y. Jones, C. Robinson and C. Dobson. The structural aspects of this grouping are further bolstered by the recent recruitment to the Wellcome Trust Centre for Human Genetics (WTCHG) of Dr S. Fuller's cryo-EM group. The juxtaposition of these biophysical based methodologies with the molecular and cellular based expertise of Professor R Phillips (Nuffield Department of Clinical Medicine; NDM) and Professor A McMichael (MRC Human Immunology Unit) underpins the crucial interdisciplinary nature of the proposal. The overall context of the proposed building is as part of a coherent development of biomedical research infrastructure planned to house the bulk of the Clinical School departments in Oxford. The site is available next to the newly completed WTCHG building on the Institute of Health Sciences Site. This position provides excellent adjacency to the X-ray crystallographic laboratories of Professors Jones and Stuart (housed within the WTCHG), as well as close proximity to the JIF funded Vaccine Centre (on the adjacent Churchill site), the MRC Human Immunology Unit at the Institute for Molecular Medicine and the NDM. The adjacency to the WTCHG gives particularly direct added value since it will allow Class 2 laboratory and computing facilities within the Structural Biology Group to complement the Class 3 facilities. In addition to the advantages conferred by the strength of the local biomedical research environment, the site has significant benefits, apropos of general accessibility, necessary for the development of a national resource. The facility is unique in aiming to house state-of-the-art cryo-EM within class 3 containment. The environmental specifications to enable optimal data collection from such equipment are already stringent for non-contained facilities. The additional constraints required for operation within class 3 containment have necessitated detailed and lengthy discussion between the building design team and the two leading Field Emission Gun cryo-EM manufacturers (Phillips and JOEL). The ability to custom design this facility has been crucial to the successful development of plans fully meeting all the criteria. The proposed building, linked by a corridor to the WTCHG, is primarily a single floor with a full-height interstitial loft to maximise access to servicing outside containment. In addition to housing the cryo-EM and associated sample preparative equipment the facility has been designed to accommodate the requirements for tissue culture, cell sorting, virus purification, virus crystallisation and mass spectrometry necessary for a unified interdisciplinary approach to the evaluation of infectious particles. These facilities will underpin the work of the applicants, supporting virological and immunological as well as biophysical analyses. The proposal includes several key pieces of state-of- the-art equipment to allow for an inter-linked set of methodologies to be brought to bear in the analysis of pathogenic agents. The provision of this array of equipment and techniques under P3 containment would be unique not only within the UK but also worldwide. When coupled with the expected provision of contained beamlines at the new UK synchrotron the proposed facility would allow for a concerted attack on the structure and function of human pathogens. Furthermore, in consultation with MAFF some additional features have been incorporated to satisfy the guidelines for MAFF category 4 pathogens. This provides the possibility of extending the scope of the facility to the most serious non-human pathogens in collaboration with the Institute of Animal Health. The role of the facility as a resource for researchers both within the UK and worldwide is formalised in the proposed management structure.
